cards.lead: Nerves traced to the brain by dissection in Ptolemaic Alexandria
cards.name: Nerves traced to the brain by dissection, Alexandria
cards.summary: Herophilus and Erasistratus dissected human bodies in Ptolemaic Alexandria and separated sensory from motor nerves, tying nerves to the brain.
cards.description: In third-century BCE Alexandria, Herophilus of Chalcedon dissected human bodies and described at least seven cranial nerves, naming six pairs. He was the first to distinguish motor from sensory nerves and spinal from cranial nerves, and he held that the brain, not the heart, was the seat of the soul.
cards.origin_note: The source calls Herophilus the first dissector in the Western medical tradition and notes that Alcmaeon of Croton earlier placed the seat of the soul in the brain.

impact.note: Scored as in the lead: the anatomy of nerves shaped Alexandrian and later medical practice, but its reach was limited to one school of physicians for centuries.

events.label: 3rd century BCE
events.statement: Herophilus, dissecting human bodies in Alexandria, distinguished motor from sensory nerves.
events.quote: He was the first to distinguish between motor and sensory nerves and also between spinal and cranial nerves.

sources.title: Herophilus of Chalcedon and the practice of dissection in Hellenistic Alexandria
sources.publisher: South African Medical Journal (excerpts reposted by Novo Scriptorium)

open_questions: Herophilus's own works are lost; the attributions here rest on later accounts. Check von Staden (1989) directly.
Erasistratus's sensory and motor distinction is not checked in the fetched text.
Galen's experiments (c. 170 CE), Alcmaeon and the Edwin Smith papyrus are not checked here.

cards.lead: Animal electricity found in nerve and muscle in Bologna
cards.name: Animal electricity in nerve and muscle, Bologna
cards.summary: Galvani's frog experiments in Bologna showed electrical effects in nerve and muscle and led him to claim a new animal electricity.
cards.description: Luigi Galvani, a professor at Bologna, found that frog torsos with metal hooks in their spines twitched. He concluded that living things produce a distinct animal electricity, and published this in his 1791 paper De viribus electricitatis in motu musculari commentarius.
cards.origin_note: The source presents Galvani's experiments and his claim of animal electricity as his own work, with no earlier claim of this kind cited.

impact.note: Scored as in the lead: the frog experiments opened electrophysiology and led to Volta's battery, with a limited direct reach at the time.

events.statement: Galvani published his paper on animal electricity in the Commentaries of the Bologna Institute of Science.
events.quote: Galvani announced his results in a long 56-page paper, “De viribus electricitatis in motu musculari commentarius” that appeared in the Commentaries of the Bologna Institute of Science in 1791.

open_questions: The 1780-1791 span of the experiments is not checked; the source dates the start to the 1770s.
The Galvani-Volta dispute is not documented from a fetched primary or scholarly source.
The du Bois-Reymond and Helmholtz measurements (1840s-1850) and the ionic explanation (1952) are later records to add with their own sources.

cards.lead: Microbes shown to cause fermentation and decay in France
cards.note: The sources support the 1857 memoir on lactic fermentation only. Decay, the 1857-1864 experiments and the earlier work of Cagniard-Latour, Schwann and Kutzing are not supported by the pages read, so the card covers fermentation alone.
cards.name: Microbes as the cause of lactic fermentation, Lille
cards.summary: Pasteur at Lille showed that a living microbe causes a specific fermentation, the first clear proof that germs cause fermentation.
cards.description: Working at Lille, Louis Pasteur traced a souring of sugar-beet fermentation to living rod-shaped microbes that crowded out yeast and turned sugar into lactic acid. His 1857 memoir, published by the French Academy of Sciences, was hailed as the initial proof that germs cause fermentation.
cards.origin_note: The source calls the 1857 memoir the initial proof that germs cause fermentation, and cites no earlier demonstration of this.

impact.note: Scored as in the lead: the microbial cause of fermentation became the basis of microbiology, pasteurisation and germ theory, in most regions.

events.statement: Pasteur's memoir on lactic fermentation, identifying a living microbe as its cause, was published by the French Academy of Sciences.
events.quote: Pasteur wrote a paper on his discovery entitled “Mémoire sur la fermentation appellée lactique” (memoir on the fermentation called lactic), which was published by the French Academy of Sciences in 1857.

open_questions: Decay (putrefaction) is not checked in the fetched text; the lead's 1857-1864 span needs the swan-neck experiments (1859-62) and the wine heating (1864) from their own sources.
Earlier findings (Cagniard-Latour, Schwann, Kutzing, 1837) and Spallanzani on spontaneous generation are not checked.
Sources differ on whether the memoir was read in 1857 or published in full in 1858; the memoir itself was not opened.

cards.lead: Induced pluripotent stem cells in Kyoto
cards.note: The sources date the mouse work to 2006 and place it at Kyoto University. The 2007 human work is not supported by a page the fetcher could open, so the card covers 2006 only.
cards.name: Induced pluripotent stem cells from mouse fibroblasts, Kyoto
cards.summary: Yamanaka's Kyoto team made mouse fibroblasts behave like embryonic stem cells with four genes, giving a route to pluripotency without embryos.
cards.description: At Kyoto University in 2006, Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi introduced four factors, Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc and Klf4, into mouse fibroblasts. The treated cells from embryonic or adult mice took on the pluripotency of embryonic stem cells, as reported in Cell.
cards.origin_note: The 2012 Nobel citation and the 2006 press release describe the reprogramming, but neither states priority, so this rests on the lead.

impact.note: Scored as in the lead: the method gave patient-specific pluripotent cells for research and therapy, with reach so far mainly among laboratories.

events.statement: Four factors made differentiated mouse fibroblasts take on the pluripotency of embryonic stem cells.
events.quote: The researchers found that four of those factors, known as Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4, could lend differentiated fibroblast cells taken from embryonic or adult mice the pluripotency normally reserved for embryonic stem cells.

events.statement: The findings were published online in the journal Cell.
events.quote: The researchers reported their findings in an immediate early publication of the journal Cell, published by Cell Press.

sources.title: With few factors, adult cells take on character of embryonic stem cells
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2012: press release

open_questions: The human iPS work of 2007 (Takahashi et al., Cell) and the parallel Wisconsin work are not checked; the lead's 2007 date needs its own source.
No fetched source states priority for the mouse 2006 result; Gurdon's nuclear transfer (1962) is cited only in the Nobel release as what it built on.
The claim that the method yields patient-specific cells for disease models and drug testing is not checked.

cards.lead: Weaver ants used to protect citrus in southern China
cards.note: The 304 CE date is reported in the fetched review, but the source of the text and its attribution are not checked, and Guangdong and Guangxi are not named in the pages read. The place is given as southern China.
cards.name: Weaver ants guarding citrus, southern China
cards.summary: Growers in southern China used weaver ants to guard citrus against pests, a practice recorded in a text dated to 304 CE.
cards.description: A text dated to 304 CE, as cited by a modern review, records the use of the weaver ant Oecophylla for pest control in China. Van Mele's review calls it the first written record of biological control and notes fewer than 70 scientific publications on the ant as a control agent in Asia from the early 1970s.
cards.origin_note: The review calls the 304 record the first written record of biological control, though it rests on a text whose attribution is not checked here.

impact.note: Scored as in the lead: a regional orchard practice with a small later research record, not a reorganisation of farming.

events.label: 304 CE
events.statement: A text dated to 304 CE is cited as the first written record of Oecophylla being used against insect pests in China.
events.quote: Oecophylla is listed as the first written record of insect predators, dating from 304 ad (Huang & Yang, 1987).

sources.title: A historical review of research on the weaver ant Oecophylla in biological control

open_questions: The attribution of the Nanfang caomu zhuang to Ji Han and its date of 304 CE are disputed in the lead; the review does not settle them. Find the earliest secure text (ninth-century sources may be safer).
Van Mele attributes the nest-selling husbandry he describes to Burma (De Bach, 1974) and says it was 'very similar' to China's; a Chinese source for the practice itself is not checked.
Whether the lead's Guangdong and Guangxi locations are supported is not checked; the place here is southern China.

cards.lead: Extinction and the succession of fossil faunas established in Paris
cards.name: Extinction and fossil succession, Paris
cards.summary: Cuvier's comparative anatomy in Paris established that fossil elephants and other animals belonged to extinct species, and that fossil faunas succeeded one another.
cards.description: In 1796 Cuvier told the National Institute of Sciences and Arts in Paris that the published studies of elephant bones contained too little detail to say whether they belonged to living species. His 1812 Recherches summarised his conclusions, and the deeper strata held giant salamanders, flying reptiles and extinct elephants that differ from living animals.
cards.origin_note: The UCMP history credits Cuvier with firmly establishing the fact of extinction; no earlier secure demonstration is cited in the sources read.

impact.note: Scored as in the lead: extinction and fossil succession reshaped palaeontology and natural history in Europe, with reach in its first decades mainly in France and Europe.

events.statement: Cuvier stated before the National Institute of Sciences and Arts in Paris the problem of fossil elephant bones.
events.quote: stated in 1796 before the National Institute of Sciences and Arts in Paris,

events.statement: Cuvier summarised his conclusions on fossil animals and the sequence of strata in his Recherches sur les ossements fossiles de quadrupèdes.
events.quote: He summarized his conclusions, first in 1812 in his _Recherches sur les ossements fossiles de quadrupèdes_

sources.title: Georges Cuvier
sources.publisher: University of California Museum of Paleontology

open_questions: The Megatherium paper of 1796 is not checked in the fetched text.
The lead's William Smith parallel (1799-1815) is not checked here and may merit its own record.
The 1808-11 Paris Basin work with Brongniart is not checked.
